clinicalPearls: Any woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain, amenorrhoea, and vaginal bleeding should be assumed to have an ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise
The great majority implant in the fallopian tube; less common sites include the cornua, ovary, cervix, caesarean scar, and abdominal cavity
Risk factors include previous ectopic pregnancy, tubal surgery or damage, pelvic inflammatory disease, endometriosis, assisted reproduction, and intrauterine contraceptive devices
Diagnosis combines serial serum beta-hCG measurement with transvaginal ultrasound; an empty uterus with a beta-hCG above the discriminatory zone raises strong suspicion
Management options are expectant, medical with methotrexate for suitable stable cases, or surgical (usually laparoscopic salpingectomy or salpingotomy)
Rupture causes intraperitoneal haemorrhage and is a life-threatening surgical emergency requiring immediate resuscitation and operative control of bleeding
A pregnancy of unknown location with rising or plateauing beta-hCG and no intrauterine gestation warrants close follow-up and a low threshold for intervention
Anti-D prophylaxis should be given to rhesus-negative women where indicated
reference.pathophysiology: An ectopic pregnancy occurs when the blastocyst implants outside the endometrial cavity, most often in a fallopian tube whose transport function has been impaired by inflammation, scarring, or altered motility. The invading trophoblast erodes the tubal wall, which lacks the capacity to accommodate a growing gestation. This leads to distension and bleeding into the tube, and eventually to tubal rupture with potentially massive intraperitoneal haemorrhage, or to tubal abortion where the products are expelled through the fimbrial end.
additionalDifferentials: Urinary tract infection or renal colic
additionalInvestigations: Serial quantitative serum beta-hCG to assess trend against expected intrauterine rise
Transvaginal ultrasound to locate the pregnancy and detect free fluid
Full blood count and blood group with cross-match if bleeding suspected
Serum progesterone as an adjunct to assess pregnancy viability in some settings
Diagnostic laparoscopy when imaging is inconclusive and suspicion remains high
redFlags: Haemodynamic instability, syncope, or signs of shock indicating ruptured ectopic with intraperitoneal haemorrhage
Severe or worsening abdominal pain with peritonism
Shoulder-tip pain suggesting diaphragmatic irritation from haemoperitoneum
Rapidly falling haemoglobin or free fluid on scan
Cervical, cornual, or scar-site implantation carrying high haemorrhage risk
reference.prognosis: With early diagnosis and treatment the maternal outlook is excellent and fertility is often preserved. Rupture remains an important cause of maternal death, especially where access to care is delayed. Women who have had one ectopic pregnancy carry an increased risk of recurrence and of subtly reduced fertility.
pitfalls: Excluding pregnancy on history alone without a beta-hCG test
Falsely reassuring interpretation of a single beta-hCG value rather than the trend
Assuming an intrauterine pregnancy excludes ectopic, missing rare heterotopic pregnancy after assisted conception
Choosing medical management without ensuring reliable follow-up
Delaying surgery in an unstable patient while awaiting investigations
management: Offer expectant management to selected stable women with low and falling beta-hCG and minimal symptoms, under close surveillance
Treat suitable stable cases medically with methotrexate, with follow-up beta-hCG monitoring to confirm resolution
Undertake surgical treatment, usually laparoscopic salpingectomy, or salpingotomy where fertility preservation is needed and the contralateral tube is damaged
In rupture, resuscitate with intravenous fluids and blood products and proceed to emergency operative control of haemorrhage as a surgical emergency
Give anti-D immunoglobulin to rhesus-negative women as indicated
Monitor serial beta-hCG after conservative, medical or salpingotomy treatment to exclude persistent trophoblast
Counsel on the increased recurrence risk and early scanning in future pregnancies, address modifiable risk factors and arrange gynaecology follow-up
